prompt: A trainee at the safety board asks which three points form the stability triangle on this sit-down counterbalanced forklift before she engages a pallet. Which supports define that triangle?

options.text: Both steer tires joined through the middle of the drive axle
The two front wheels and the pivot of the rear axle
Both fork tips paired with the middle of the counterweight
Four tire contact patches drawn as a rectangular support base

explanation: On this counterbalanced forklift the stability triangle is the two front wheels and the pivot of the rear steer axle. The combined center of gravity has to stay inside that triangle.

distractorExplanations.a: This reverses the triangle: the base is the front wheels and the apex is the rear-axle pivot, not the middle of the drive axle.
distractorExplanations.c: Fork tips and the counterweight are not the support points that define the stability triangle on this forklift.
distractorExplanations.d: Three-point suspension makes a triangle. Four tire patches do not form the support base on a counterbalanced truck.

prompt: After the carriage climbs nearly to mast top inside a narrow warehouse aisle, the lead asks what that high position changes on the machine. What rises along with the freight?

options.text: The center of gravity and the risk of a tip
The rated capacity printed for this machine
Rear-wheel traction and overall stability
The horizontal load-center distance on the forks

explanation: Raising the freight lifts the combined center of gravity and increases tip risk. The high carriage in this aisle does not add capacity or rear-wheel traction.

distractorExplanations.b: This confuses a higher carriage with more capacity. Raising freight derates the lift; it does not increase the printed rating.
distractorExplanations.c: A high load lightens the rear wheels. It does not improve rear-wheel traction or overall stability in this aisle.
distractorExplanations.d: Load center is the horizontal distance from the fork face. Lift height changes center-of-gravity height, not that distance.

prompt: With a pallet already seated on the forks, she angles the mast backward before rolling away from the pick face. What does that backward tilt accomplish for stability?

options.text: It shifts the combined center of gravity forward over the forks
It helps keep the center of gravity inside the triangle
It makes travel acceptable while the freight stays fully raised
It increases the rated capacity shown on the data plate

explanation: Tilting the mast back with the pallet seated moves the combined center of gravity rearward and helps keep it inside the stability triangle before she leaves the pick face.

distractorExplanations.a: Back tilt moves the combined center of gravity rearward, toward the drive axle, not forward over the forks.
distractorExplanations.c: Back tilt does not authorize travel with the freight fully raised. The pallet still needs to come down before she rolls.
distractorExplanations.d: Mast tilt does not change the capacity on the data plate. The rating stays what the manufacturer marked.

prompt: Between two rack rows he initiates a sharp corner while the pallet remains elevated near the upper beam. How does that corner with the load elevated change tip exposure?

options.text: It greatly increases the risk of a tip
It stays acceptable if the steering input is gentle
It lowers the combined center of gravity in the corner
It mainly creates a forward tip instead of a side tip

explanation: A sharp corner with the pallet still elevated greatly increases tip risk, because the high center of gravity is pushed toward the side of the stability triangle.

distractorExplanations.b: Gentle steering does not remove the tip risk of a corner taken with the pallet still near the upper beam.
distractorExplanations.c: The corner does not lower the center of gravity. It pushes that high mass toward the side of the triangle.
distractorExplanations.d: This corner produces a lateral tip risk. A forward tip comes from hard braking or too much forward tilt.

prompt: A yard supervisor reviewing near-miss cards asks which routine handling choice most increases sideways overturn chance on this sit-down machine. Which condition drives the combined mass toward a side edge?

options.text: Rolling along with the forks kept just above the floor
Sitting parked with the parking brake fully applied
Turning on a slope or hauling an off-center load
Waiting with the mast vertical and the forks empty

explanation: Lateral tip risk rises when the machine turns on a slope or hauls an off-center load, because those conditions drive the combined mass toward a side of the triangle.

distractorExplanations.a: Forks kept low on a straight run is the stable travel setup. It does not drive the mass toward a side edge.
distractorExplanations.b: A parked machine with the brake set is not the turning or off-center condition that raises lateral tip risk.
distractorExplanations.d: An empty mast sitting vertical does not create the sideways overturn this supervisor is asking about.

prompt: Before accepting an unfamiliar crate, the lead taps the metal nameplate on the cowl and asks which capacity figure that nameplate is meant to state. What does that nameplate list?

options.text: A maximum that applies at every fork position
The calendar date of the latest full inspection
Rated capacity at the stated load center
Battery voltage standing in for a load rating

explanation: The nameplate lists rated capacity at a stated load center. It is not a maximum for every fork position, an inspection date, or a battery-voltage substitute for the rating.

distractorExplanations.a: The nameplate rating applies at the stated load center, not as one maximum for every position of the forks.
distractorExplanations.b: Inspection dates live in the maintenance record. The nameplate states capacity at a stated load center.
distractorExplanations.d: Battery voltage may appear on a separate label. It does not replace rated capacity at the stated load center.

prompt: This pallet matches the previous weight, yet its balance point now sits farther from the vertical fork face than the dimension shown on the rating tag. What does that extended balance point do to allowable weight?

options.text: It increases the capacity the machine may carry
It reduces the capacity the machine may carry
It leaves rated capacity unchanged for this lift
It removes tip risk while the freight is raised

explanation: Moving the balance point farther from the fork face than the rating tag states reduces the weight this machine may carry. A longer load center does not increase capacity.

distractorExplanations.a: A balance point farther out reduces capacity. It does not let the machine carry more than the rating tag allows.
distractorExplanations.c: The rating is not unchanged. Once the balance point exceeds the stated dimension, allowable weight goes down.
distractorExplanations.d: A longer balance point increases forward tip risk. It does not remove tip risk while the freight is raised.

prompt: Halted at the pick slot, he runs the lateral positioner and slides a dense unit toward one carriage end before depositing it. What can that lateral movement do to the machine?

options.text: It moves the unit alone and leaves the machine center fixed
It can move the center of gravity sideways, so use care
It is appropriate while the machine is already rolling
It shortens the forward load-center distance from the fork face

explanation: Sliding a dense unit to one carriage end can move the combined center of gravity sideways, so the operator uses care while the machine is stopped at the slot.

distractorExplanations.a: The dense unit is part of the combined mass. Sliding it sideways moves the machine's center of gravity too.
distractorExplanations.c: The positioner should be used while halted at the slot. Doing it while rolling adds lateral instability.
distractorExplanations.d: Lateral movement does not shorten the forward load center, which is measured out from the fork face.

prompt: Freight-trailer creep has opened a visible gap at the bumper, yet he continues rolling straight at the exposed lip. What chief hazard follows if the machine leaves that dock lip?

options.text: Greater stability once the drive wheels drop
A fall or a tipover off the dock
A higher rated capacity as the wheels leave the plate
Automatic leveling that keeps the freight secure

explanation: If the machine leaves the dock lip, the hazard is a fall or a tipover. An open gap at the bumper does not improve stability or raise the rated capacity.

distractorExplanations.a: Dropping the drive wheels off the lip destroys stability. It does not make the machine steadier once the wheels drop.
distractorExplanations.c: Leaving the plate does not raise rated capacity. The hazard is a fall or a tipover, not a bigger rating.
distractorExplanations.d: Nothing levels the mast by itself if the machine leaves the dock lip. The freight is not kept secure.

prompt: During orientation a recruit compares this sit-down unit against a narrow-aisle stacker and asks how counterbalance machines offset fork weight. What provides that offset?

options.text: Rear weight that offsets the load on the forks
Outriggers that reach out and straddle the freight
Extra ballast bolted onto the front drive wheels
Mast tilt alone, without a separate counterweight

explanation: A counterbalanced machine uses rear weight to offset the load on the forks. Outriggers belong to other designs, and mast tilt does not replace the counterweight.

distractorExplanations.b: Outriggers that straddle freight belong on reach and straddle designs, not on this counterbalance unit.
distractorExplanations.c: The offsetting weight sits at the rear, behind the drive axle, not as ballast on the front wheels.
distractorExplanations.d: Mast tilt cradles a load but does not replace the rear counterweight that offsets fork weight.

prompt: Students stand where a pantograph reach model is parked beside a conventional sit-down model, and instruction covers how the reach model stays upright. How do those support layouts differ?

options.text: Outrigger stability versus a sit-down counterbalance
A heavier rear counterweight than the sit-down model uses
An exemption from OSHA powered-truck training rules
A capacity set by battery size rather than load center

explanation: A reach truck stays upright through its outrigger layout, which differs from the rear-counterweight design of a sit-down counterbalanced truck. OSHA 1910.178 training still applies to both.

distractorExplanations.b: A reach model does not stay upright by using a heavier rear counterweight than the sit-down model.
distractorExplanations.c: OSHA 1910.178 training covers reach trucks and sit-down trucks. The reach model is not exempt from those rules.
distractorExplanations.d: Reach capacity is still a rated load at a stated load center, not a figure taken from battery size.

prompt: Carrying freight, she approaches the inclined warehouse approach and must decide fork direction before climbing. Which direction should the forks face while that freight is aboard?

options.text: Downhill while the truck is carrying a load
Uphill on a trip when the forks are empty
Uphill when the truck is carrying a load
Across the slope to steady the freight

explanation: With freight aboard, the forks face uphill on the incline so the load points upgrade. Pointing the load downhill, or crossing the slope, is the miss on this approach.

distractorExplanations.a: Pointing the forks downhill while freight is aboard puts the load downgrade, which is the miss on this incline.
distractorExplanations.b: Empty forks point downhill. This trip has freight aboard, so the load faces uphill instead of the empty-fork heading.
distractorExplanations.d: Crossing the slope invites a lateral tip. The approach is taken straight, with the load facing upgrade.

prompt: Carriage still elevated, he hits the service brake because a walker steps out of a cross aisle. What can that abrupt halt do to the elevated freight and the machine?

options.text: It settles the freight and steadies the machine
It raises how much weight the machine may carry
It can tip the machine forward
It is the required finish for every elevated move

explanation: A hard brake application with the carriage still elevated can tip the machine forward. The abrupt halt does not settle the freight or raise the weight the machine may carry.

distractorExplanations.a: An abrupt halt with the carriage elevated throws the freight forward. It does not settle or steady the machine.
distractorExplanations.b: Braking does not change rated capacity. The risk here is a forward tip, not a higher allowable weight.
distractorExplanations.d: A sudden stop with the load still up is a hazard, not a required way to finish an elevated move.

prompt: He must transport a bulky crate projecting well beyond both fork sides through a congested aisle junction. What additional caution may that bulky crate require on this move?

options.text: Slower turns, plus a spotter where the swing is tight
Travel with the crate raised so it clears the rack beams
No extra caution wherever the machine body can fit
A mirror glance before each corner on the route

explanation: A bulky crate that projects past the forks may need slower turns and a spotter where the swing is tight. Raising it, or relying on a mirror glance, does not control that swing.

distractorExplanations.b: Raising the bulky crate moves the mass up and widens the swing. It still needs to travel low through the junction.
distractorExplanations.c: Aisle fit does not cancel the swing of a projecting crate. The move still needs slower turns and a spotter.
distractorExplanations.d: A mirror glance does not show the full swing past the fork sides. Tight spots need a spotter and slower turns.

prompt: While hoisting, the tail grows light and the steering tires feel ready to unload from the pavement. What does that light tail indicate, and what action comes next?

options.text: Hoist higher so the missing weight returns to the steer axle
Capacity or center-of-gravity trouble, so lower and reposition
Have a coworker stand on the counterweight to restore balance
Tilt the mast forward and continue to the drop-off point

explanation: A light tail means the load may exceed capacity or the center of gravity is too far forward. He should lower the freight and reposition it, not hoist higher or add a rider.

distractorExplanations.a: Hoisting higher moves the mass up and forward, which lightens the tail further instead of restoring the steer axle.
distractorExplanations.c: A person on the counterweight is not an allowed fix. The freight must come down and be repositioned.
distractorExplanations.d: Forward tilt pushes the mass farther forward and worsens the light tail he already feels on the steer tires.

prompt: At receiving, a coworker claims this machine can accept the dense coil simply because the upright looks tall enough. Where must real capacity be read before the coil is lifted?

options.text: Guess it from how tall the upright looks next to the coil
Copy the rating from a different machine used last week
Use the coil shipping weight as if it were the machine rating
Read the data plate on the truck

explanation: Capacity is read on the truck data plate, not guessed from how tall the upright looks beside the coil. Mast height is not a capacity rating under OSHA 1910.178.

distractorExplanations.a: This treats mast height as capacity. The upright can look tall and still be over its plate rating for this coil.
distractorExplanations.b: Another machine's rating does not transfer. This truck's own data plate is the capacity he must read.
distractorExplanations.c: Shipping weight says what the coil weighs, not what this machine is allowed to lift at this load center.

prompt: Halfway toward an upper beam, the carriage keeps climbing with freight aboard and the hoist lever stays held. What does continued hoisting do to stability as the freight goes higher?

options.text: The center of gravity rises and a tip grows more likely
The center of gravity drops and the tip chance disappears
The center of gravity stays put no matter how high it goes
Rated capacity climbs because the mast is now extended farther

explanation: As the carriage climbs, the raised freight moves the center of gravity up and makes a tip more likely. Continued hoisting does not lower that center or raise rated capacity.

distractorExplanations.b: Continued hoisting raises the center of gravity. It does not drop that center or make a tip less likely.
distractorExplanations.c: Height is not neutral. As the freight goes higher, the combined center of gravity moves up with it.
distractorExplanations.d: Extending the mast does not increase rated capacity. Capacity falls as lift height and tip risk increase.

prompt: The run ends at a blind corner and the unit remains high after clearing the beam he just left. What sequence belongs before any steering input at that corner?

options.text: Steer through the corner while the unit is still up high
Lower the load first, then turn
Raise the unit farther so the corner has extra clearance
Tilt the mast forward and pivot while the load stays high

explanation: He should lower the load and only then turn. Steering through the blind corner while the unit is still high is the miss, even if the beam is already cleared.

distractorExplanations.a: Turning while the unit is still high is the miss at this blind corner. The load comes down before the steering input.
distractorExplanations.c: More height does not buy a safer corner. It raises the mass and makes the turn less stable.
distractorExplanations.d: Forward tilt with the load still high moves the mass forward during the pivot, which is the opposite of the right sequence.

prompt: Descending the outdoor approach with freight aboard, a coworker urges her to aim the forks toward the lower end. Which way should that freight face on this incline?

options.text: Downgrade, forks aimed at the lower end of the approach
Across the slope so both drive wheels share the incline
Upgrade, with the load facing uphill
Whichever heading reaches the dock door in fewer moves

explanation: On this incline with freight aboard, the load faces upgrade. Aiming the forks toward the lower end puts the load downhill, which is the miss under OSHA 1910.178.

distractorExplanations.a: Forks aimed at the lower end put a loaded truck downgrade. On this incline the freight must face uphill.
distractorExplanations.b: Crossing the incline is a lateral-tip setup. The freight should face upgrade, not sit across the slope.
distractorExplanations.d: Fewer moves to the door does not set fork direction. With freight aboard, the load faces up the incline.

prompt: Mid-slope on the inclined approach he spots a parked hand truck and begins swinging around it while drive wheels remain on the slope. What choice keeps the machine stable?

options.text: Swing a wide arc so the freight stays centered on the slope
Turn toward the high end because the tail holds the inside
Turn toward the low end and let the grade pull the forks around
Do not turn while still on the ramp

explanation: He should not turn while the drive wheels are still on the ramp. Swinging around the hand truck on the slope is the lateral-tip miss.

distractorExplanations.a: A wide arc is still a turn on the ramp. He should not swing around the hand truck while the wheels are on the slope.
distractorExplanations.b: Turning toward the high end is still a turn on the grade. The stable choice is not to turn here at all.
distractorExplanations.c: Letting the grade pull the forks around is still a turn on the ramp, and it adds a downhill component.

prompt: Almost the entire dense casting rests on one fork while the mate fork stays nearly bare as he prepares to depart the staging lane. What must occur before departure?

options.text: Restack so the weight is not heavy on one side
Depart anyway, since a side-heavy load is stable in a straight line
Slide the counterweight toward the light fork and then depart
Drop the bare side and carry the casting on one fork

explanation: A casting that is heavy on one fork moves the center of gravity sideways. He restacks it so the weight is shared before he departs the staging lane.

distractorExplanations.b: A straight line does not cancel a sideways center of gravity. The casting has to be restacked before departure.
distractorExplanations.c: The counterweight is fixed. He cannot slide it to the light fork to correct a one-sided casting.
distractorExplanations.d: Carrying the casting on one fork keeps the mass off center. The fix is to restack so both forks share it.

prompt: With a carton clamp mounted, the paper roll sits farther forward than bare forks allowed on yesterday's job. Which capacity marking deserves trust for today's pick?

options.text: The original bare-fork number, ignoring the clamp entirely
The attachment plate, not the bare-fork number
The roll weight alone, because a clamp does not derate anything
The largest figure printed on the overhead guard decal

explanation: The clamp moves the load center out and derates the truck. He uses the attachment plate, not the original bare-fork number alone, for today's pick.

distractorExplanations.a: The bare-fork number ignores the clamp, which moved the load center out and derated this truck.
distractorExplanations.c: Knowing the roll weight is not enough. The clamp changes capacity, so the attachment plate governs this pick.
distractorExplanations.d: A decal on the overhead guard is not the attachment rating. The clamp's own plate is the figure to trust.

prompt: A coworker climbs the rear counterweight to read a high label and claims that rider also increases allowable capacity for the following pallet. How should that counterweight be treated?

options.text: A rider there is acceptable when the person holds the overhead guard
The rider counts as extra rated capacity for the next pallet
Not a step, and not spare capacity
Usable as a step once the parking brake is set and the forks are down

explanation: The counterweight is not a step and it is not spare capacity. A rider on it does not increase the allowable load for the following pallet.

distractorExplanations.a: Holding the overhead guard does not make the counterweight a step. He should not climb it to read the label.
distractorExplanations.b: A rider is not added capacity. The plate rating does not increase because someone stands on the counterweight.
distractorExplanations.d: The parking brake and lowered forks do not turn the counterweight into a step or into spare capacity.

prompt: On the daily inspection he finds a drive tire flat with the tread separating from the carcass. What action is required before any freight is moved on this machine?

options.text: Add air at the next break if the opposite tire still looks sound
Keep operating, because a flat tire leaves stability unchanged
Hoist the carriage so the damaged tire bears less of the freight
Tag the truck out; the tire changes stability

explanation: A flat tire with separating tread changes stability. He tags the machine out of service before anyone moves freight on it, as OSHA 1910.178 requires for an unsafe truck.

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting to add air leaves a flat, separating tire in service. That tire already changes stability, so the truck is tagged out.
distractorExplanations.b: A flat tire does change stability. Keeping the machine in service treats a bad tire as if the counterweight setup were normal.
distractorExplanations.c: Raising the carriage does not unload a damaged drive tire safely. The machine stays out of service until the tire is repaired.

prompt: Preparing for a long run across the building, he is choosing carriage height for the loaded trip. How should the forks be carried while the machine is traveling?

options.text: Just clear of the floor, mast tilted back
Mast fully raised for the whole trip so nothing overhead is struck
Dragged along the floor so the pallet cannot shift on the forks
Held level with the operator's shoulders the entire way

explanation: For the trip he carries the forks just high enough to clear the floor, with the mast tilted back. Traveling with the mast fully raised is the miss on this run.

distractorExplanations.b: Mast fully raised for the trip is the miss. The forks stay just high enough to clear the floor, tilted back.
distractorExplanations.c: Dragging the forks on the floor is not the travel position. They clear the floor, with the mast tilted back.
distractorExplanations.d: Shoulder height is still a raised load for a long run. Travel height is just clear of the floor, tilted back.

prompt: After the pickup the lateral shifter remains fully stroked to the right, and he is ready to drive off. What should happen to that freight before the trip starts?

options.text: Leave the shifter at the carriage end and drive away
Center the load before you travel
Stroke the shifter farther out so the aisle mirror can see it
Hoist to full height and center the freight while already moving

explanation: He centers the freight on the carriage before travel. Leaving the lateral shifter stroked to the right keeps the load off center for the whole trip.

distractorExplanations.a: Leaving the shifter at the end of the carriage is the miss. The freight is centered before he drives off.
distractorExplanations.c: More offset for a mirror does not center the load. The shifter comes back to center before the trip.
distractorExplanations.d: Centering while already moving, at full height, combines a high load with an off-center mass. Center it before travel.

prompt: Because the crate overhangs both forks, a helper proposes balancing it on the tips to avoid locating an attachment. What is the proper method for that overhanging crate?

options.text: Balance the crate on the fork tips and take it across
Have the helper steady the overhang by hand during the move
Lay a second pallet across the tips to widen the support
Use the right attachment, not the tips

explanation: A crate wider than the forks needs the right attachment. Balancing it on the tips is the miss, even if that avoids a search for the attachment.

distractorExplanations.a: Balancing the overhanging crate on the tips is the miss. A load wider than the forks needs the right attachment.
distractorExplanations.b: A helper's hands are not an attachment. A crate wider than the forks needs the rated attachment, not someone walking beside it.
distractorExplanations.c: A second pallet across the tips is not the rated attachment. He uses the attachment meant for a wide crate.

prompt: The bridge plate lies unsecured between the trailer and the dock, and nobody has verified a rating for this loaded machine. What must be true before he crosses on it?

options.text: Secured, and rated for this truck
Safe to cross if the plate looks thick enough for one trip
Acceptable while loose, provided the trailer brakes stay set
Optional, because every dock plate is interchangeable

explanation: The bridge plate has to be secured and rated for this loaded machine before he crosses. A loose or unverified plate is not ready under OSHA 1910.178.

distractorExplanations.b: Looking thick enough is not a rating, and one trip does not replace securing the plate before he crosses.
distractorExplanations.c: Trailer brakes do not secure a loose bridge plate. The plate itself must be secured and rated for the truck.
distractorExplanations.d: Dock plates are not interchangeable. This one must be secured and rated for the loaded machine.

prompt: Turning left out of a storage row, he has a walker tight against the tail corner of the machine. Why is that tail corner hazardous during this steering maneuver?

options.text: The machine pivots at the cab center, so the tail barely moves
The forks swing out, while the tail is supposed to track inside
The steer axle is locked, so the tail follows the fork path exactly
The rear swings wide; the pivot is not the cab center

explanation: In this turn the rear of the machine swings wide, and the pivot is not the center of the cab. The walker at the tail corner is inside that swing.

distractorExplanations.a: The pivot is the rear steer axle, not the cab center, so the tail does not stay put in this left turn.
distractorExplanations.b: The tail does not track inside while the forks swing out. On this truck the rear swings wide in the turn.
distractorExplanations.c: The steer axle is what pivots. The tail does not follow the fork path, which is why the walker is in danger.

prompt: As a lateral overturn starts, his instinct is to bail toward the side where the freight is falling. What should he do instead of bailing out that side?

options.text: Jump toward the falling freight so you clear the mast
Stand on the seat and pull the overhead guard to shift your weight
Tilt the mast hard forward to dump the freight off the forks
Stay with the truck and lean away from the fall

explanation: If the freight starts to fall, he stays with the truck and leans away from the fall. Jumping toward the falling side puts him where the freight is going.

distractorExplanations.a: Jumping toward the falling freight puts him on the fall side. He stays in the machine and leans away from that side.
distractorExplanations.b: Standing on the seat to shift weight leaves the truck. He stays seated and leans away from the falling side.
distractorExplanations.c: Tilting the mast forward to dump the freight makes the fall worse. He stays with the truck and leans away.

prompt: At the start of your shift you walk around a sit-down counterbalance truck in the grocery cooler before anyone assigns you a move. Which parts belong on that pre-use inspection?

options.text: Tires, forks, mast, chains, leaks, horn, lights, and brakes
Whatever the shop flagged at the last planned maintenance visit
The horn by itself, since yesterday's walkaround already passed
Battery water and the seat adjustment left for the weekly shop route

explanation: The pre-use inspection on this cooler truck covers tires, forks, mast, chains, leaks, horn, lights, and brakes before you take a move. A shop list, a horn tap, or battery water alone leaves the rest of that exam undone.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the daily pre-use exam with the planned maintenance list; the tires, forks, mast, chains, leaks, horn, lights, and brakes are still checked.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses yesterday's pass with this shift's exam; a horn-only glance skips tires, forks, and brakes that can change overnight.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a fluid top-off with the safety exam; battery water and a seat tweak do not replace forks, chains, brakes, and lights.

prompt: A receiver spots a hairline crack where the left fork blade meets the heel on a truck staged at dock three. What should happen to that truck before the next pickup?

options.text: Keep the pickup going until the next planned maintenance window
Remove the truck from service for the cracked or bent fork
Weld the crack at the dock, then finish the remaining pickups
Limit this truck to lighter pallets so the crack carries less

explanation: A crack or bent heel on the fork is damage found before the next pickup, so the truck is removed from service. Waiting for maintenance, welding at the dock, or switching to lighter pallets leaves a bad fork under a load.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a cracked or bent fork with an item that can wait for planned maintenance; the truck is removed from service now.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a dock weld with an approved repair; a cracked fork is removed from service rather than welded and sent back to work.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a damaged fork with a load you can lighten yourself; a crack or bent heel is not kept in service on lighter pallets.

prompt: You lower the empty carriage and see a fresh drip of hydraulic fluid forming under the lift cylinder on a truck nobody has used yet today. What is the right call before you take a load?

options.text: Fix the hydraulic leak before the truck is used
Top off the reservoir and continue if the drip stays slow
Write the drip down and repair it after the last load today
Treat a seep as ordinary wear on an older lift cylinder

explanation: A fresh drip under the lift cylinder is a hydraulic leak on a truck that has not worked yet today, so it is fixed before anyone takes a load. Topping off, logging it for later, or blaming the truck's age leaves the leak in service.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses topping up the reservoir with a repair; a leak can drop the load, so it is fixed before the truck is used.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a later log entry with the rule that a hydraulic leak is corrected before anyone takes a load on this truck.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses truck age with an acceptable seep; an older lift cylinder does not make a fresh drip safe to drive.

prompt: Maintenance left a note that leaf-chain stretch on this turret truck must follow the builder's interval, and your shift is the one that runs it first. How should those chains and their anchors be checked?

options.text: Inspect the chains and anchors on the OEM schedule
Wait to inspect them until a chain actually fails in use
Lubricate the chains and skip any wear or stretch check
Look at the chains and anchors during the annual shop visit

explanation: Leaf chains and their anchors on this turret truck are inspected on the maker's schedule, which is what the maintenance note is pointing at. Waiting for a break, oiling without a check, or saving it for a yearly visit is not that OEM interval.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a failure investigation with inspection; chains and anchors are checked on the maker's schedule, not after a chain breaks.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses lubrication with inspection; oiling a chain does not measure stretch or show a worn anchor on the OEM schedule.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the annual shop visit with the maker's interval; a once-a-year look is not inspecting chains and anchors per the OEM.

prompt: Before you nose a loaded truck out of the battery-charge lane into the main cross-aisle, you tap the horn button and glance at the headlights. What must those devices do on this check?

options.text: The horn and the lights must work when you test them
They become optional once the brakes have already been tested
